q: Between 1871 and 1918 the region belonged to another country, which pushed its growers toward high volumes of cheap blending wine. Which country?
opts: Belgium
Switzerland
Germany
Austria
exp: Annexation after the Franco-Prussian War turned the vineyard into a bulk supplier. Quality returned slowly after 1918, and the region was annexed a second time between 1940 and 1945.

q: Full AOC status arrived here far later than in Bordeaux or Burgundy. In which year?
exp: Two annexations and two wars left the region's rules unwritten while the rest of France was being classified in the 1930s. The delay is the reason the Grand Cru tier is younger still.

q: Riquewihr, Kaysersberg and Gewurztraminer all point the same way linguistically. Which heritage?
opts: Flemish, from the medieval cloth trade
Romance, closest to Occitan
Celtic, surviving in place names alone
Germanic, in the Alemannic dialect
exp: Alsatian is an Alemannic German dialect, and it supplies most of the village, vineyard and grape names in the region. The wines are French; the vocabulary is not.

q: Biodynamic and organic farming are unusually widespread here by French standards. Which practical factor helps?
opts: Organic certification is a legal condition of the appellation
The dry, sheltered climate keeps fungal pressure down
Subsidies forbid conventional treatments
Fungal disease is entirely absent from the region
exp: Less rain means less mildew and rot, so cutting back sprays is far more practical than on the Atlantic coast. Several of the region's leading estates converted decades ago.

q: A thin base spread with cream, onion and bacon comes out of a wood oven during a cellar visit. What is the dish?
opts: Tarte flambee
Baeckeoffe
Choucroute garnie
Kougelhopf
exp: Flammekueche is the Alsatian name and tarte flambee the French one. It is the standard food of a cellar visit, eaten with Sylvaner, Pinot Blanc or a glass of Cremant.

q: Drive north from Adelaide, or inland from any coast, and the vines give out long before the desert begins. What pins Australian viticulture to a crescent along the southern and south-eastern rim of the continent?
opts: The soils of the interior are too fertile to give quality fruit
The interior is too hot and dry and the tropical north too wet
Federal law restricts vineyard planting to land within one hundred kilometres of the coast
Phylloxera has made the whole inland unplantable
exp: Most of the continent is desert or tropical savannah, and a vine needs a warm but not relentless season plus a winter cold enough for dormancy. That combination exists only around the cooler southern rim and on the highlands standing behind it.

q: Reading a map of the country's vineyards from north to south, almost every one falls inside a band roughly twelve degrees of latitude wide. Which band?
opts: About fifteen to twenty-seven degrees south
About twenty to thirty-two degrees south
About thirty-eight to fifty degrees south
About thirty-one to forty-three degrees south
exp: The Hunter and the Swan sit at the warm northern end and southern Tasmania at the cool southern one. Mirrored into the northern hemisphere that band would run from North Africa to Provence, which is why Australia's cool sites are usually made rather than found.

q: Orange sits at a latitude that ought to bake its fruit, yet the Chardonnay comes in with acidity intact and alcohol moderate. What is doing the cooling?
opts: The Southern Ocean, which lies only a few kilometres away
Height: the vineyards climb the flanks of an extinct volcano
Persistent cloud drifting down from the tropics
Irrigation drawn from cold mountain rivers
exp: Every hundred metres of elevation costs roughly half a degree of mean temperature, and nights at height fall further still. Australia uses altitude the way Europe uses latitude, which is how a region well north of Melbourne ends up cooler than one south of it.

q: Three hot districts strung along one inland river system depend entirely on irrigation and supply the fruit behind a great deal of everyday Australian wine. Which three?
opts: Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Geelong
Barossa Valley, Clare Valley and Eden Valley
Riverland, Murray Darling and Riverina
Margaret River, Great Southern and Pemberton
exp: The Murray and the Murrumbidgee make farming possible in country otherwise too dry for it. Their fruit is ripe, soft and cheap to grow, and it is the backbone of the multi-region blends sold under the broadest Geographical Indications.

q: A grower in Bordeaux would need a dispensation to run water to the vines; across most of Australia a dripline is standard equipment. What explains the difference?
opts: Australian soils hold no water whatever the rainfall
European rules ban irrigation everywhere, while Australia has no water regulation at all
Rainfall is low and falls mostly outside the growing season
Australian law obliges growers to irrigate in order to guarantee a yield
exp: Much of the Australian vineyard receives less growing-season rain than a vine needs, and a dry summer is the norm rather than a crisis. Nothing in Australian wine law restricts irrigation, and across much of the country it is the only way to farm at all. The water itself is another matter: it is licensed and allocated as a scarce resource rather than argued over as a quality question, which inverts the European approach.

q: Hundred-year-old Shiraz still stands on its own roots in South Australia, and the state stops travellers at its border to check for vine cuttings, vineyard equipment and even soiled boots. What is being kept out?
opts: Downy mildew, which the dry climate otherwise prevents
Fruit fly, which attacks the ripening bunches
Pierce's disease, which arrived late last century
Phylloxera, which has never reached the state
exp: Phylloxera reached Victoria and New South Wales in the nineteenth century but never crossed into South Australia, so its vineyards were never grafted onto American rootstock. That quarantine is the reason some of the oldest producing vines on earth are South Australian.

q: Barossa Valley appears in large letters on a front label, yet nothing on the bottle commits the producer to a grape, a yield, a ripeness minimum or a day in oak. What does an Australian Geographical Indication actually promise?
opts: That the wine followed a set of rules on variety and ageing written for that place
That yields were held below a stated maximum
That the wine passed an official tasting panel before release
Only that the fruit was grown in the named place
exp: A GI is a statement of origin and nothing else, which is the fundamental difference between this system and a French appellation. What is planted, how it is farmed and how it is made are left entirely to the producer, so the name tells you where and never how.

q: High Eden lies inside Eden Valley, which lies inside Barossa, which lies inside South Australia. Reading those four from the smallest outward, what are the tiers called?
opts: Region, subregion, zone, state
Subregion, zone, region, state
Subregion, region, zone, state
Commune, region, zone, state
exp: A region must demonstrate measurable homogeneity and a minimum scale of production, and a subregion must be more homogeneous still. A zone has to satisfy neither test, which is why a zone can be enormous and tell a buyer very little.

q: One Australian Geographical Indication reaches across state lines and turns up on inexpensive bottles blended from fruit picked a thousand kilometres apart. Which?
opts: Central Ranges
Mount Lofty Ranges
South Eastern Australia
Limestone Coast
exp: South Eastern Australia takes in the whole of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania along with the grape-growing parts of Queensland and South Australia. It exists to give the cross-state blend a legal name, and it is why one brand can hold its style through a difficult vintage anywhere.

q: A winemaker wants Coonawarra, a single vintage year and Cabernet Sauvignon all printed on the front label. Each of those three claims must hold true of at least how much of the wine?
opts: Ninety-five percent
All of it
Eighty-five percent
Seventy-five percent
exp: One threshold covers origin, vintage and variety alike, so a Coonawarra Cabernet may legitimately carry fifteen percent of another grape from another place. The claim is verified through the winery's records rather than by tasting the wine.

q: A label reads Semillon Sauvignon Blanc rather than Sauvignon Blanc Semillon, and the wine inside is those same two grapes either way. What does the running order tell a buyer?
opts: The first grape came from the named region and the second from elsewhere
The first grape named was the first to be fermented
The order is decorative and carries no meaning at all
The varieties are listed from the largest component down
exp: Australia requires a multi-variety label to run from the largest component down, so the name is a recipe read left to right. A wine labelled Shiraz Cabernet holds more Shiraz than Cabernet, and reversing the words on the label would mean reversing the blend.
